section.title: The Reign of Joash
section.sectionRationale: As long as Jehoiada the priest lives, Joash faithfully repairs the temple through a nationwide collection. But after Jehoiada's death, Joash abandons the LORD for Asherah poles and idols, and when Jehoiada's own son Zechariah is raised up by the Spirit to rebuke the nation, Joash has him stoned to death in the temple courtyard. Aram then defeats Judah's much larger army, and Joash himself is assassinated on his sickbed by his own servants.
section.thesis: Joash's reign shows that reform inherited from a mentor's influence is not the same as a heart truly given to God, for once Jehoiada is gone Joash abandons the LORD so completely that he murders the very prophet who warned him, and the same measure he showed Zechariah is measured back to him in his own violent end.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Joash repairs the temple under Jehoiada's guidance, verses 1 to 14; Jehoiada's death and burial with the kings, verses 15 to 16; Joash's apostasy and the murder of Zechariah, verses 17 to 22; and Judah's defeat by Aram and Joash's assassination, verses 23 to 27.

units.label: Joash repairs the temple
units.note: he set his heart on repairing

verses.text: Joash was seven years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem forty years. His mother's name was Zibiah; she was from Beersheba.
And Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest.
Jehoiada took for him two wives, and he had sons and daughters.
Some time later, Joash set his {{lev|heart}} on repairing the house of the LORD.

So he gathered the priests and Levites and said, "Go out to the cities of Judah and collect the money due annually from all Israel, to repair the house of your God. Do it quickly." The Levites, however, did not make haste.

So the king called Jehoiada the high priest and said, "Why have you not required the Levites to bring from Judah and Jerusalem the tax imposed by Moses the servant of the LORD and by the assembly of Israel for the Tent of the Testimony?"
For the sons of that wicked woman Athaliah had broken into the house of God and had even used the sacred objects of the house of the LORD for the Baals.
At the king's command a chest was made and placed outside, at the gate of the house of the LORD.
And a proclamation was issued in Judah and Jerusalem that they were to bring to the LORD the tax imposed by Moses the servant of God on Israel in the wilderness.
All the officers and all the people rejoiced and brought their contributions, and they dropped them in the chest until it was full.

Whenever the chest was brought by the Levites to the king's overseers and they saw that there was a large amount of money, the royal scribe and the officer of the high priest would come and empty the chest and carry it back to its place. They did this daily and gathered the money in abundance.

Then the king and Jehoiada would give the money to those who supervised the labor on the house of the LORD to hire stonecutters and carpenters to restore the house of the LORD, as well as workers in iron and bronze to repair the house of the LORD.
So the workmen labored, and in their hands the repair work progressed. They restored the house of God according to its specifications, and they {{chazaq|reinforced}} it.

When they were finished, they brought the rest of the money to the king and Jehoiada, and with it were made articles for the house of the LORD, utensils for the service and for the burnt offerings, dishes, and other objects of gold and silver. Throughout the days of Jehoiada, burnt offerings were presented regularly in the house of the LORD.
When Jehoiada was old and full of years, he died at the age of 130.
And Jehoiada was buried with the kings in the City of David, because he had done what was good in Israel for God and His temple.
After the death of Jehoiada, however, the officials of Judah came and paid homage to the king, and he listened to them.
They abandoned the house of the LORD, the God of their fathers, and served the Asherah poles and idols. So wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem for this guilt of theirs.
Nevertheless, the LORD sent prophets to bring the people back to Him and to testify against them, but they would not listen.

Then the {{ruach|Spirit}} of God came upon Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest, who stood up before the people and said to them, "This is what God says: 'Why do you transgress the commandments of the LORD so that you cannot prosper? Because you have forsaken the LORD, He has forsaken you.'"
But they conspired against Zechariah, and by order of the king, they stoned him in the courtyard of the house of the LORD.

Thus King Joash failed to {{zakar|remember}} the kindness that Zechariah's father Jehoiada had extended to him. Instead, Joash killed Jehoiada's son. As he lay dying, Zechariah said, "May the LORD see this and call you to account."

units.label: The death of Joash
units.note: his own servants conspired against him

verses.text: In the spring, the army of Aram went to war against Joash. They entered Judah and Jerusalem and destroyed all the leaders of the people, and they sent all the plunder to their king in Damascus.

Although the Aramean army had come with only a few men, the LORD delivered into their hand a very great army. Because Judah had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers, judgment was executed on Joash.

And when the Arameans had withdrawn, they left Joash severely wounded. His own servants conspired against him for shedding the blood of the son of Jehoiada the priest, and they killed him on his bed. So he died and was buried in the City of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.
Those who conspired against Joash were Zabad son of Shimeath the Ammonitess and Jehozabad son of Shimrith the Moabitess.

The accounts of the sons of Joash and the many pronouncements about him, and of the restoration of the house of God, are indeed written in the Treatise of the Book of the Kings. And his son Amaziah reigned in his place.

lev.gloss: Heart. Joash sets his lev on repairing the temple, showing genuine early devotion; the tragedy of his reign is that the heart set on God's house under Jehoiada's influence does not remain fixed on God once that influence is gone.

chazaq.gloss: To strengthen, repair, or reinforce. The workmen chazaq, reinforce, the temple structurally; the same root elsewhere means to be strong or courageous, a wordplay the chapter's tragedy underlines, since Joash reinforces a building while his own heart grows weak toward God.

ruach.gloss: Spirit, wind, or breath. The ruach of God comes upon Zechariah, empowering him to speak God's own indictment; that the king murders the very prophet raised up by God's own Spirit shows the full depth of Joash's apostasy.

zakar.gloss: To remember. Joash failed to zakar, remember, the kindness Jehoiada had shown him; the same root elsewhere describes God remembering His covenant, making Joash's forgetfulness of a human benefactor's kindness a bitter contrast to the LORD's own faithful remembering of His promises.

basic.context: Joash reigns well for many years, faithfully organizing a nationwide collection to repair the temple, as long as his mentor Jehoiada the priest is alive to guide him. But once Jehoiada dies, the officials of Judah persuade Joash to abandon the LORD's temple for Asherah poles and idols. When Jehoiada's own son Zechariah, moved by God's Spirit, publicly rebukes the nation's unfaithfulness, Joash orders him stoned to death in the very temple courtyard his father had served. Aram then defeats Judah's much larger army, wounding Joash, and his own servants finish the job by assassinating him on his sickbed, in direct retribution for Zechariah's blood. He is buried, like Jehoram before him, outside the tombs of the kings.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative tracing the tragic arc of a king whose reform depended on someone else's godliness rather than his own settled devotion to the LORD. It is not a claim that mentorship or good influence is worthless, but a sober warning that reform inherited from another person's faithfulness must become one's own conviction, or it will collapse the moment that influence is removed.
basic.originalLanguages: Joash sets his lev, heart, on repairing the temple, real devotion for a time. The workmen chazaq, reinforce, the building itself even as the king's own resolve weakens once Jehoiada is gone. When the ruach, Spirit, of God empowers Zechariah to speak a final warning, Joash's response, having the very son of his benefactor stoned, exposes just how completely he had forsaken the LORD.
basic.typology: Zechariah, the righteous son of a faithful priest, killed in the temple courtyard by the very king he served and warned, stands among the innocent blood the Old Testament remembers, and Jesus Himself names Zechariah's murder alongside Abel's as bookending the violence done to God's righteous messengers, pointing forward to His own unjust death at the hands of those He came to save.
basic.christ: Jesus explicitly names Zechariah son of Berechiah, likely this same Zechariah or closely connected to him, alongside Abel as marking the full measure of righteous blood shed in Israel's history, Matthew 23:35, showing that this murder in the temple courtyard is remembered by Christ Himself as a paradigm of how God's people can kill their own faithful witnesses. Zechariah's dying plea, may the LORD see this and call you to account, anticipates the far greater contrast of Christ's own dying words, Father, forgive them, showing the surpassing mercy of the cross beyond even righteous demand for justice.
basic.god: God is patient, sending prophet after prophet to call His wandering people back before raising up Zechariah with a final, Spirit empowered word. Yet God is also just; He remembers Zechariah's innocent blood and brings Joash to account through the very army he might have defeated and the very servants who should have protected him, showing that forsaking the LORD carries consequences that eventually catch up even a once faithful king.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Kings 12 gives the parallel account of Joash's temple repairs. Matthew 23:35 names the blood of Zechariah son of Berechiah as part of the righteous blood required of that generation. Luke 23:34 contrasts Zechariah's dying plea for justice with Christ's dying plea for mercy, Father, forgive them. Galatians 6:7 states plainly that whatever a man sows he will also reap, fulfilled exactly in Joash's own violent end.
basic.oneStory: Joash's reign, faithful while his mentor lived and then catastrophically apostate once that influence was removed, culminating in the murder of a Spirit filled prophet and Joash's own violent death, warns every reader that borrowed faith is not saving faith. This tragedy of righteous blood shed in the temple courts anticipates the far greater righteous blood shed at Calvary, where the dying plea shifts from a cry for justice to a cry of forgiveness that reaches even those who shed it.

context.literary:
The chapter is hinged precisely at Jehoiada's death, verses 15 to 16, which stands as a literary seam almost exactly at its midpoint, fourteen verses of faithful repair before it and eleven verses of apostasy and its consequences after. Everything before the seam is measured, deliberate, and successful. Everything after it accelerates rapidly toward disaster, a pattern of narrative pacing that mirrors its own content, patient construction giving way to sudden collapse.

The Chronicler also builds a careful irony around the word house. Joash sets his heart on repairing the house of the LORD, verse 4, organizes a nationwide collection for it, and by verse 14 the workmen have restored the house of God according to its specifications. Yet the very next scene shows Judah's officials leading the king to abandon that same house, verse 18, so that the building Joash personally restored stands as the structural, physical rebuke of the heart that abandoned it. His own murdered prophet dies in the courtyard of that very restored house, verse 21, closing the irony completely.

The chapter's ending also participates in the Chronicler's consistent practice of using burial notices as final verdicts on a reign. Joash is buried in the City of David but explicitly not in the tombs of the kings, verse 25, the identical judgment already passed on the wicked Jehoram, 21:20, and the identical judgment that will later fall on Ahaz, 28:27. Compared with the parallel account in 2 Kings 12, which never mentions Zechariah at all, Chronicles alone preserves this episode, a deliberate addition that turns a fairly neutral royal record in Kings into a moral drama the Chronicler clearly wants his post-exilic readers to feel.
context.historical:
The temple repair follows a tax explicitly rooted in the wilderness census offering, Exodus 30:11 to 16, a half shekel required of every Israelite twenty years and older as ransom money for their lives, originally collected once for the tabernacle's construction. Joash and Jehoiada revive it as an ongoing maintenance levy, collected in a chest set at the temple gate rather than gathered directly by priests, a practical mechanism that let ordinary worshipers give as they came to the temple rather than waiting for a formal census. The text notes the repairs were needed because Athaliah's own sons had earlier broken into the house of God and used its sacred objects for the Baals, verse 7, meaning Joash's collection was restoring a building actively looted, not merely aged.

Jehoiada's death at 130 stands out even among Israel's most honored figures. Moses died at 120, Deuteronomy 34:7, and Aaron at 123, Numbers 33:39, both remarkable lifespans by any ancient reckoning. Jehoiada exceeds them both, and the text calls him old and full of years, verse 15, before recording that he alone among non royal figures in Judah was buried with the kings in the City of David, because he had done what was good in Israel for God and His temple, verse 16, an honor Chronicles gives no other priest.

The military disaster that follows also has a specific backdrop. The parallel account in 2 Kings 12:17 to 18 records that Hazael king of Aram had already captured Gath and turned toward Jerusalem, and that Joash bought him off by stripping the temple treasury, the very treasury he himself had once labored to fill. Chronicles omits that bribery and instead records only that a small Aramean raiding party defeated a far larger Judean army, verses 23 to 24, framing the same military crisis not as a matter of Aram's strength but as the LORD's own judgment executed through a token force.
context.canonical:
The qualifying phrase all the days of Jehoiada the priest, verse 2, belongs to a recurring device the Chronicler uses to measure a king's heart rather than merely his actions. Uzziah two chapters later is said to have sought God as long as Zechariah his mentor lived, and God gave him success, 26:5, almost the identical structure applied to a different mentor and a different king. Both notices warn the reader in advance that a reign shaped this heavily by another person's influence has not yet been tested on its own, and both kings go on to prove the warning true in strikingly different ways, Joash through murder and apostasy, Uzziah through pride and unlawful worship.

This chapter also preserves what became, in the traditional ordering of the Hebrew Bible, the last murder of a righteous messenger named in the entire canon. Chronicles stands as the final book of the Hebrew Scriptures as Jesus and His hearers knew them, so when Jesus says the blood of all the prophets shed since the foundation of the world will be charged to His generation, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who was killed between the altar and the sanctuary, Luke 11:50 to 51, He is naming the first murder in Genesis and the last murder in Chronicles, spanning the whole of Israel's Scriptures from beginning to end in a single accusation. Zechariah's death in this chapter therefore carries a canonical weight far beyond its own narrative, standing as the final entry in a list of innocent blood that Christ Himself will complete and answer at the cross.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The Chronicler wants his readers to feel the shock of the turn at verse 17 as sharply as possible, which is why he gives fourteen careful verses to Joash's patient, successful temple repair before collapsing the king's devotion in a single sentence the moment Jehoiada is gone. His purpose is not merely to record a sad history but to press a specific warning on a post-exilic community rebuilding its own worship under foreign rule and, in many cases, under borrowed spiritual leadership from priests, scribes, and governors who would not always be present to guide them. Reform inherited from someone else's godliness must become one's own settled conviction, or it will not survive that person's absence.

He also wants the connection between ingratitude and violence drawn starkly. Joash failed to remember the kindness Jehoiada had extended to him, verse 22, the priest who had literally saved his infant life, and that forgetfulness becomes, within a single chapter, murder. The author intends his readers to see how quickly a debt of love unacknowledged can curdle into active harm against the very family that showed it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records one king's specific collapse. It does not teach that every believer raised under a godly mentor will necessarily abandon the faith once that mentor dies, nor that mentorship itself is dangerous or to be avoided. Many figures in Scripture, Joshua under Moses, Elisha under Elijah, Timothy under Paul, carry a mentor's faith forward faithfully for a lifetime.

What the chapter does teach, by simple and sober description, is a real pattern worth heeding: devotion that has never been tested apart from another person's presence is an unknown quantity, not yet proven either way. The chapter also plainly describes, without commanding as a model, both a costly and effective act of generosity, the temple collection, and a costly and horrifying act of injustice, Zechariah's murder, leaving the reader to draw the obvious moral conclusion from each without the text needing to state it directly.

debates.question: Was Joash ever genuinely faithful, or was his early reign merely political conformity to Jehoiada's power?

views.label: Genuine, if dependent, early faithfulness
views.case: Verse 2 states plainly that Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, and his own initiative in verse 4, setting his heart on repairing the temple, and his rebuke of the Levites' slowness in verse 6, suggest real personal engagement, not mere passive conformity.

views.label: Faithfulness contingent entirely on external influence
views.case: The qualifying phrase all the days of Jehoiada the priest, verse 2, and the totality of his collapse the moment Jehoiada dies, suggest his righteousness was never deeply rooted in his own heart but was sustained entirely by his mentor's presence and authority.

debates.bearing: Either way, the chapter's central warning stands. Whatever the depth of Joash's early sincerity, it did not survive the removal of external influence, illustrating the difference between reform imposed or modeled by others and conviction that endures on its own.

debates.question: Is the Zechariah Jesus names in Matthew 23:35 the same Zechariah killed in this chapter?

views.label: Yes, the same figure
views.case: Jesus describes his death as happening between the altar and the sanctuary, Luke 11:51, matching the temple courtyard setting of verse 21 exactly, and most conservative commentators read son of Berechiah as either a scribal variant, a grandfather's name, or a second name for Jehoiada, since Chronicles is the last historical martyrdom recorded in the Hebrew canon's final book, fitting Jesus's span from Abel to Zechariah precisely.

views.label: A different figure
views.case: Some note that a Zechariah son of Berechiah is elsewhere identified as the minor prophet of Zechariah 1:1, and point to a Zechariah son of Baruch killed in the temple decades later during the Jewish war against Rome, recorded outside Scripture, as a possible alternative referent, though that event happened after Jesus spoke these words, which complicates the identification.

debates.bearing: Whichever identification is correct, Jesus is treating the killing described in this chapter as characteristic and paradigmatic of Israel's repeated rejection of God's messengers. The shared location and manner of death make it unmistakable that this event, at minimum, stands behind His words.

study.originalLanguages:
The Chronicler's verdict in verse 2, Joash did what was right, yashar, in the eyes of the LORD, uses the standard formula by which every king of Judah and Israel is measured throughout both Kings and Chronicles. Yashar means straight or level, the opposite of crooked or twisted, and the qualifying phrase that follows, all the days of Jehoiada the priest, quietly warns that a life yashar under someone else's guidance has not yet proven itself yashar on its own. The word describes an outward course more than an inward root, which is exactly the ambiguity the rest of the chapter exposes.

When the officials of Judah lead the nation into Asherah worship, verse 18, the text says wrath, qetsef, came upon Judah and Jerusalem for this guilt. Qetsef is the Chronicler's characteristic word for covenant anger, the same term used of Uzziah's fury against the priests two chapters later, 26:19, and of the wrath that nearly fell on Jehoshaphat's alliance with Ahab, 19:2. The word marks divine displeasure that is provoked, specific, and covenantal, never arbitrary. It answers a particular breach rather than expressing generalized divine temper.

Verse 20 says the Spirit of God came upon Zechariah, but the Hebrew verb behind came upon is more vivid than the English suggests. It is labash, to clothe or put on, the same verb used when the Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon, Judges 6:34, and when the Spirit clothed Amasai before he pledged himself to David, 1 Chronicles 12:18. The Spirit does not merely visit Zechariah from outside. He is described as garments the prophet puts on, wrapping him entirely for the single, costly task of speaking God's indictment to the very king who owed his throne to Zechariah's own father.

The conspiracy formed against Zechariah in verse 21, they conspired, qashar, uses the identical root behind Athaliah's own cry of qesher, treason, two chapters earlier, 23:13. The word choice is exact and pointed. The very charge Athaliah threw, falsely, at the people who restored the rightful king becomes, without comment from the narrator, the true description of what Joash and his officials do to the rightful prophet. The conspirators against Zechariah are doing precisely what Athaliah accused others of doing, real qesher against the LORD's own anointed order, this time carried out by the king himself.

typology.type: The priest's own son, killed in the temple courtyard his father had spent a lifetime serving and restoring
typology.fulfillment: Zechariah dies at the hand of the very king his father had rescued, crowned, and served, killed in the courtyard of the temple his family had spent generations maintaining. Stephen, centuries later, names this exact pattern to the Sanhedrin just before his own death, asking which of the prophets their fathers did not persecute, Acts 7:52, and is then stoned outside the city by the very council entrusted with Israel's worship. Christ Himself is rejected and killed by the leaders of the very temple He came to cleanse and fulfill, John 2:19 to 21, the same tragic shape repeating at its highest and final pitch.

typology.type: Zechariah's dying plea, may the LORD see this and call you to account, verse 22
typology.fulfillment: Zechariah's final words ask God to see his murder and hold his killers accountable, a right and lawful cry for justice from an innocent victim. Stephen, facing the same death by stoning, instead prays, Lord, do not hold this sin against them, Acts 7:60, deliberately echoing and reversing Zechariah's plea. Christ's own dying words go further still, Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do, Luke 23:34, so that the trajectory from Zechariah's courtyard to Calvary to Stephen's stoning traces the gospel's own movement from justly demanded judgment to freely offered mercy.

typology.type: Joash's failure to remember the kindness Jehoiada had shown him, verse 22
typology.fulfillment: Joash forgets, and that forgetting becomes murder. The very phrase used, he did not remember, stands in the sharpest possible contrast to how God treats those He has redeemed. Under the new covenant God promises, their sins and lawless acts I will remember no more, Hebrews 8:12, choosing not to hold His people's worst failures against them, exactly the mercy Joash refused to extend to Jehoiada's son. Where human gratitude fails and turns to violence, God's own remembering runs the opposite direction, holding onto kindness shown and releasing wrongs committed.

study.christ:
This chapter's darkest moment becomes one of the clearest lines Jesus Himself draws from the Hebrew Scriptures to His own generation. Naming the full sweep of Israel's rejection of God's messengers, Jesus says the blood of all the prophets will be charged to this generation, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who was killed between the altar and the sanctuary, Luke 11:50 to 51, and Matthew's parallel names him Zechariah son of Berechiah, Matthew 23:35. Whatever the precise identification behind that patronymic, the manner and location of the death Jesus describes matches this chapter exactly, and Jesus is treating Zechariah's murder as the paradigm case of Israel killing its own messengers, a pattern about to reach its full and final expression in His own crucifixion at the hands of the very city He came to save.

The Spirit's brief, decisive clothing of Zechariah, verse 20, also points toward Christ by way of contrast. Zechariah is clothed with the Spirit for a single message and a single costly moment. John says of Jesus that God gives the Spirit without limit, John 3:34, an unbroken, permanent anointing rather than a momentary empowering for one urgent task. Every prophet clothed briefly with God's Spirit across the Old Testament, Gideon, Amasai, Zechariah, points forward to the one man who carries that Spirit fully and always.

Zechariah's dying words also anticipate Christ by contrast rather than simple correspondence. May the LORD see this and call you to account, verse 22, is a right and lawful cry for justice, and God does answer it in the chapter's own final verses, judgment falling on Joash through Aram's invasion and his own servants' conspiracy. But Christ's dying prayer moves past even righteous demand for justice into free mercy, Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do, Luke 23:34, absorbing the very violence that would otherwise demand a reckoning. Stephen, dying the same death Zechariah died, consciously prays in the manner of Christ rather than the manner of Zechariah, Lord, do not hold this sin against them, Acts 7:60, showing that Christ's cross had already begun to reshape how His people meet unjust death.

Finally, Joash's forgetting stands as a dark mirror to Christ's remembering. Jehoiada's kindness toward Joash, saving his infant life and restoring him to the throne, should have bound the king to Jehoiada's family in lasting gratitude, yet Joash forgot it entirely, verse 22. Christ, by contrast, having loved His own who were in the world, loved them to the very end, John 13:1, and secures for His people a new covenant in which God says of their sins and lawless deeds, I will remember them no more, Hebrews 8:12. Where Joash's forgetting produced violence against the innocent, Christ's remembering produces mercy toward the guilty.
study.god:
God's patience runs through this chapter even at its darkest point. Before Zechariah ever speaks, the LORD sent prophets to bring the people back to Him and to testify against them repeatedly, over time, and they would not listen, verse 19, plural messengers and repeated appeals long before the single, final, fatal word Zechariah delivers. Judgment in this chapter is never impulsive. It arrives only after patience has been thoroughly and repeatedly refused.

God's justice is also shown to work through ordinary military and political events rather than only through direct supernatural stroke. Verse 24 states plainly that although the Aramean army came with only a few men, the LORD delivered into their hand a very great army, because Judah had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers, judgment was executed on Joash. The verse deliberately separates cause from mechanism. Aram's small raiding force is the visible means, but the LORD's own verdict against Joash's apostasy is the stated cause, so that a modest military skirmish becomes, in the Chronicler's telling, an act of direct divine judgment. The same pattern continues in Joash's assassination, carried out by his own servants for entirely human motives, shedding the blood of the son of Jehoiada, verse 25, yet placed by the narrator within the same unbroken sequence of consequence for forsaking the LORD.

God is also shown here as the one who empowers weak and costly obedience. The Spirit's clothing of Zechariah, verse 20, comes at the very moment speaking up will be fatal, and God does not spare His messenger from the cost His own Spirit's message provokes. Zechariah is given the courage to speak, not exemption from the consequence of speaking. This is a sober but consistent biblical pattern, that being filled with God's Spirit is no guarantee of physical safety, only of faithfulness to the word God gives.

Finally, God's character is revealed in what He does not do as much as what He does. He does not strike Joash down the instant Zechariah dies, nor does He immediately restore the nation the moment its sin is named. Judgment on Joash comes only after further time has passed, an invading army, a wound, a slow death on a sickbed at the hands of his own household, showing a God whose justice is certain but never hurried, willing to let consequences ripen in their own season rather than forcing an immediate reckoning that might satisfy human demand for swift retribution but would show less of His own patient, deliberate character.

crossReferences.note: The parallel account of Joash's reign omits Zechariah's murder entirely and instead records that Hazael of Aram was bought off with temple treasure rather than defeated by a small raiding force, 12:17-18. Chronicles alone adds Zechariah's death and its theological framing, showing its distinct concern to explain events as consequences of covenant unfaithfulness.

The original half shekel tax, a ransom for each life at the wilderness census, funded the tabernacle's service. Joash and Jehoiada revive the same levy centuries later as an ongoing maintenance fund for Solomon's temple, showing how a law given for one generation's needs could be lawfully extended to meet another's.

The Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon, using the identical Hebrew verb behind the Spirit coming upon Zechariah in verse 20. Both men are wrapped by the Spirit for a single, urgent, costly task, Gideon to deliver Israel by the sword, Zechariah to deliver God's word regardless of the cost to himself.

Jesus names the righteous blood of Zechariah son of Berechiah as part of the full measure of innocent blood His generation will answer for, a direct reference back to the murder this chapter records, whatever the precise identification behind the patronymic given.

Jesus specifies that this Zechariah was killed between the altar and the sanctuary, language matching the courtyard setting of verse 21 exactly, and pairs him with Abel as the first and, in the traditional ordering of Hebrew Scripture, the last martyred prophet named in the entire canon.

Stephen accuses the Sanhedrin of the same pattern this chapter shows, persecuting and killing God's messengers, immediately before he is stoned in a manner that deliberately echoes both Zechariah's death and Christ's own dying prayer of forgiveness.

The new covenant promise that God will remember His people's sins no more stands in direct contrast to Joash's failure to remember Jehoiada's kindness, verse 22. Where Joash's forgetting became violence, God's gracious refusal to remember guilt becomes the ground of mercy.

Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return, fulfilled with almost mechanical precision in Joash's own story, sowing the murder of an innocent son and reaping his own murder at the hands of his own servants within the same chapter.

Jehoram, Joash's own great grandfather, dies to no one's regret and is buried in the City of David but not in the tombs of the kings, the identical formula later applied to Joash himself, verse 25, marking both as kings whose reigns the Chronicler refuses to honor with full royal burial.

study.oneStory:
Joash's reign folds two opposite stories into a single life. For roughly the first half of his forty years he embodies exactly what chapter 23 promised, a rightful king restoring the LORD's house and honoring the man who saved him. For the second half he embodies exactly what Athaliah represented, a throne turned against the LORD's own worship and against the LORD's own messenger. The same movement that opened this account of restored kingship closes with that restoration nearly undone from within, not by a foreign usurper this time but by the very king who had once seemed its clearest proof.

This is the Bible's recurring warning that reform received is not the same as reform rooted. Israel's whole history under the judges and the kings repeats the pattern on a national scale, faithfulness under a strong leader collapsing into apostasy once that leader is gone, and Joash compresses the entire cycle into one reign and one telling verse, all the days of Jehoiada the priest. The murder of Zechariah marks the moment the pattern turns from mere neglect into active violence against God's own word, a moment so significant that Jesus Himself reaches back across the whole of Israel's Scriptures to name it alongside the very first murder in Genesis.

The chapter's bleakness is not the last word, even within its own logic. Zechariah's dying plea for justice does not go unanswered. Judgment does reach Joash, but the deeper answer to this chapter waits centuries further on, when another son is killed near an altar by the very people he came to save, and instead of crying for justice prays for mercy on His killers. What Joash forgot, the kindness that saved his life, Christ never forgets, and the new covenant He establishes remembers His people's sins no more even as it remembers, and answers, every drop of righteous blood shed since Abel.

quiz.q: How long did Joash do what was right in the eyes of the LORD?

options.text: All the days of Jehoiada the priest, suggesting his faithfulness depended heavily on Jehoiada's living influence.
options.note: Verse 2 gives this exact qualifying phrase, which the rest of the chapter shows to be significant.

options.text: For his entire forty year reign without exception.
options.note: The text explicitly qualifies his righteousness to the days of Jehoiada, and he apostatizes completely after the priest's death.

options.text: Only for the first seven years of his life before becoming king.
options.note: The qualifying phrase concerns the days of Jehoiada's life, not merely Joash's childhood before his reign began.

options.text: The text gives no indication of how long his righteousness lasted.
options.note: Verse 2 explicitly qualifies his righteous conduct to the days of Jehoiada the priest.

quiz.q: How was the temple repair actually funded?

options.text: Through a nationwide collection using a chest placed at the temple gate, filled by the willing contributions of the people.
options.note: Verses 8 to 11 describe this collection method and the people's generous response.

options.text: Entirely from the king's personal treasury with no public involvement.
options.note: The text describes a public, nationwide collection effort, not funding solely from the king's private resources.

options.text: By melting down existing temple furnishings.
options.note: New articles were made once repairs were finished, but the funding itself came through the collected tax, not melted furnishings.

options.text: No method of funding the repairs is described.
options.note: Verses 5 to 11 give a detailed account of the collection method.

quiz.q: What happened after the death of Jehoiada the priest?

options.text: The officials of Judah persuaded Joash to abandon the temple and serve Asherah poles and idols instead.
options.note: Verses 17 to 18 record this sudden and complete apostasy immediately following Jehoiada's death.

options.text: Joash continued exactly as before, with no change in his devotion.
options.note: The text explicitly records a dramatic reversal into idolatry, not a continuation of his prior faithfulness.

options.text: Joash appointed a new high priest to continue Jehoiada's reforms.
options.note: Rather than continuing reform, the text records Joash's abandonment of the temple for idolatry.

options.text: No change in Judah's worship is recorded after Jehoiada's death.
options.note: Verses 17 to 18 explicitly record a dramatic change toward idolatry.

quiz.q: How did Joash respond to Zechariah's Spirit empowered rebuke?

options.text: He ordered Zechariah stoned to death in the courtyard of the house of the LORD, forgetting the kindness of Zechariah's father Jehoiada.
options.note: Verses 21 to 22 record this murderous response and its stark contrast to Jehoiada's earlier kindness to Joash.

options.text: He repented immediately and restored true worship.
options.note: The opposite occurred; Joash had Zechariah killed rather than repenting at his warning.

options.text: He exiled Zechariah from Jerusalem rather than killing him.
options.note: The text specifically records Zechariah's execution by stoning, not exile.

options.text: He ignored Zechariah's warning with no further action.
options.note: Verse 21 records the specific, violent action taken against Zechariah.

options.text: Aram defeated Judah's larger army and wounded him, then his own servants assassinated him on his bed in retribution for Zechariah's blood.
options.note: Verses 23 to 25 record this exact sequence of military defeat and assassination.

options.text: He died peacefully of old age after a long and secure reign.
options.note: The text explicitly describes a violent military defeat followed by assassination, not a peaceful death.

options.text: His son Amaziah overthrew him in a coup.
options.note: The conspirators are named as Zabad and Jehozabad, his own servants, not his son Amaziah, who succeeded him afterward.

options.text: The text does not describe how his reign ended.
options.note: Verses 23 to 25 give a detailed account of his defeat and assassination.

questions: Joash's faithfulness seemed to depend heavily on Jehoiada's living influence rather than his own settled conviction. Whose influence is currently holding your own faith together, and how might God be calling you to make that faith genuinely your own?
The officials of Judah persuaded Joash toward idolatry the moment his mentor was gone. What voices are waiting for a weak moment to pull you away from what you know is right?
Zechariah spoke God's word at great personal cost, and it cost him his life. Where is God calling you to speak an unwelcome truth, even if it may cost you something?
Joash forgot the kindness Jehoiada had shown him and repaid it with violence. Is there someone whose past kindness to you deserves more gratitude and honor than you are currently giving it?

Joash's story ends in the very consequences he brought on Zechariah. Where do you need to trust that God sees injustice, even when it goes unaddressed for a season, and will call every account to settle in His own time?

translationNotes.note: The tax imposed by Moses refers to the half shekel wilderness census tax of Exodus 30:11-16, here reapplied as an ongoing temple maintenance collection under Joash.

This Zechariah, son of Jehoiada the priest, is distinct from the minor prophet Zechariah of the postexilic period; Jesus' reference in Matthew 23:35 to Zechariah son of Berechiah has occasioned some discussion, since this Zechariah is called son of Jehoiada, though many understand the names to refer to the same historical figure or a close relation within the priestly family.

For shedding the blood of the son of Jehoiada the priest follows the Septuagint and Vulgate reading; most Hebrew manuscripts read of the sons, plural, though the singular fits the immediate narrative concerning Zechariah specifically.
